title: The night of the senses
hookLine: when prayer stops feeling good, God may be weaning us from the sweets
last: MY HOUSE BEING NOW AT REST.

cards: People who pray don't always say this out loud. At the start, it can feel wonderful. Mass, a quiet church, a psalm read slowly, and something warm comes.
Tears, sometimes. Peace. Going back is easy.
Then one day it's just gone. Show up, say the words. Nothing.
Flat as cardboard. It's easy to conclude that something went wrong, or that God has left, or that it was never real. John of the Cross had a very different explanation.

teach.h: A MOTHER FEEDS HER BABY MILK.
teach.b: First, the mother. John opens his book the Dark Night with a homely picture. A loving mother holds her baby close, warms it, and feeds it sweet milk.
That's how God treats beginners in prayer, he says: with comfort and sweetness. Second, the weaning. But a mother who loves her child doesn't nurse it forever.

teach.h: THEN SHE WEANS IT TO WALK.
teach.b: One day she weans it. She sets it down so it will learn to walk, and it cries for the milk.
Saint Paul says something similar to one young church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet." John says God does the same with souls.
The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so they can grow. Third, the sweet tooth. John is funny and sharp about beginners.

He lists their faults in prayer: wanting more and more good feelings, a spiritual sweet tooth; judging others who seem less devout; sulking when prayer is dull. The night of the senses is God's cure for all that.
When the feelings dry up, you find out whether you were seeking God, or the sweets God gave.

teach.h: I GAVE YOU MILK TO DRINK, NOT MEAT.
teach.b: Dryness in prayer, John says, can be a sign that God is closer, not farther, doing the work quietly, below what you can feel. He doesn't say every dry spell is this; tomorrow he gives ways to tell.
But he says: don't assume God left because the sweetness did.

how: Catholic spiritual directors often turn to John's Dark Night, book one, when people say prayer has gone dry, and encourage them to keep praying faithfully rather than chasing feelings.

o: a reward God keeps for only the holiest saints
the joy of finally reaching union with God
the comfort God gives beginners in prayer

games.q: what's inside the night — tap the pairs.
p: can be a sign God is closer

games.q: you've prayed every day for a year, and it used to feel wonderful. now it feels like nothing. what does John say?
o: you've done something wrong; stop until you find it.
God may be weaning you from the sweets; keep going.
games.why: John says God takes the sweetness away so the soul can grow, the way a mother weans a child. dry is not gone.

practice: Pray even if it's dry: sit, breathe, and don't try to make anything happen. If you pray, just be with God, even if it feels like talking to a wall; that counts.
If you don't, sit with something you've been faithful to that doesn't feel exciting anymore, a friendship, a job, a promise, and notice that showing up still matters.

wordCard.voice: Sweetness. The comfort God gives beginners in prayer, which the night of the senses takes away, the way a mother weans a child, so the soul can grow. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: dry is not gone. A mother weans the child she loves. Two hundred sixty-one days in.
